title: Hank's Night in the Sun

jokes.text: Artie's speech about black sneakers vs. black dress shoes, ending with 'Ok? Got it? Dig it? Dismissed.'
jokes.setup: Artie delivers a stern, military-style dressing-down to the staff about footwear — treating proper shoe color as a matter of career survival.
jokes.punchline: The absurd seriousness with which he treats shoe color ('You'll need 'em because I'll chase your delicate little butt right out into the street') combined with the incongruously hip sign-off 'Dig it? Dismissed.'
jokes.explanation: A strong cold-open character beat. The comedy is entirely in Artie's voice — the hyper-authoritative tone applied to a trivially small grievance is pure Rip Torn. 'Delicate little butt' is unexpectedly tender. 'Dig it? Dismissed' is a generational code-switch that feels organically Artie. High character integration because only Artie could make this land.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: The next time one of you shows up wearing black sneakers instead of black dress shoes, you'll need 'em because I'll chase your delicate little butt right out into the street.

jokes.text: 'Who dropped out, George Wendt or Angela Lansbury?'
jokes.setup: Paula bursts in panicked saying they're in 'deep shit.' Artie, unfazed, immediately assumes the worst-case late-night scenario.
jokes.punchline: His first instinct is a guest cancellation — the mundane industry crises are so routine to him that he rattles off two wildly mismatched celebrity names (a Cheers barfly and a British dame) as if they're equivalent.
jokes.explanation: Sharp economy — one line that reveals Artie's world-weary industry experience, establishes the guest lineup, and gets a laugh from the incongruity of the pairing. Very well constructed.

dialogue.line: Because he thinks if you can see the colors, it's easier to pick the flavor.

jokes.text: 'Why does Larry have to go into the yogurt place in person?' / 'Because he thinks if you can see the colors, it's easier to pick the flavor.'
jokes.setup: Larry is violently ill from frozen yogurt. Artie asks why Larry was even there.
jokes.punchline: Larry's neurotic, pseudo-logical reasoning for his own presence — he's so controlling and paranoid he can't even delegate a yogurt run, and his justification is absurdly specific.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant capsule characterization. The joke is entirely about Larry's neurosis — the idea that he needs to personally verify yogurt colors is so precise in its absurdity that it's both funny and deeply true to who Larry Sanders is. High character integration: this couldn't describe any other character on TV.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Thank god, because I've seen Larry vomit. It's not something you want to watch over and over again on Hard Copy.

jokes.text: 'He threw up all over the front seat of Beverly's car, and then he threw up all over Ventura Boulevard.' / 'Sherman Oaks?' / 'Studio City.' / 'Any witnesses?'
jokes.setup: Paula describes Larry's vomiting episode in escalating detail.
jokes.punchline: Artie's first instinct is not concern for Larry but damage control — asking which neighborhood (as if it matters for PR) and immediately whether there are witnesses.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first genuinely excellent joke. The 'Sherman Oaks/Studio City' beat is a perfect misdirect — he's not clarifying for geographic reason, he's assessing exposure. Then 'Any witnesses?' lands the true punchline: Artie's entire worldview is crisis management. The rhythm is impeccable: three short exchanges, escalating absurdity, and the deadpan payoff. Genuinely well-crafted sitcom writing.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You're right. Flop Howie and Louie, bump Saget from third to fourth, and make sure that Seinfeld knows that he's our first choice.

jokes.text: 'Thank god, because I've seen Larry vomit. It's not something you want to watch over and over again on Hard Copy.'
jokes.setup: Paula confirms no witnesses to Larry's public vomiting incident.
jokes.punchline: Artie's relief is framed not in terms of dignity but in terms of tabloid TV — the specific image of Hard Copy running vomit footage on repeat is both vivid and darkly funny.
jokes.explanation: Artie's media-literacy cynicism in one line. 'Over and over again on Hard Copy' is perfectly specific — it's not just 'the press,' it's the exact format of exploitation tabloid TV. Feels lived-in and real for the character and the era.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: When he says no, make sure that Richard Lewis thinks that he's our first choice, and so on down the list.

jokes.text: Artie's priority list for guest hosts: 'Jerry Seinfeld, Richard Lewis, Bob Saget, John Ritter, Howie Mandel, Louie Anderson.'
jokes.setup: Artie needs to find a guest host in 45 minutes and rattles off a ranked list.
jokes.punchline: The list itself is funny as a snapshot of 1994 late-night bench depth — it starts strong (Seinfeld) and degrades fast, bottoming out at Louie Anderson. The casual specificity of the rankings is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the curation and the implicit insult ladder. Louie Anderson as the bottom of a list that starts with Seinfeld is a period-specific industry joke that lands for anyone familiar with the era's comedy hierarchy.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Oh, your mind amazes me!

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm just now comfortable with it myself.

jokes.text: 'Make sure that Seinfeld knows he's our first choice. When he says no, make sure that Richard Lewis thinks he's our first choice, and so on down the list.' / 'Oh, your mind amazes me!'
jokes.setup: Artie gives instructions on how to manage each declining comedian's ego.
jokes.punchline: The cynical meta-instruction reveals the entire late-night ego-management game as a systematic lie — and Paula's genuine admiration of Artie's manipulative genius is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: A sharp industry-insider joke. The protocol of making every descending choice feel like a first choice is a real Hollywood practice, and articulating it this nakedly is both satirically cutting and funny. Paula's 'Your mind amazes me' is the perfect straight-man response that makes Artie's amorality look like genius.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: 80% unemployment in the acting ranks, you can't find me one name?

jokes.text: 'I'm just now comfortable with it myself.'
jokes.setup: Paula says Artie's mind amazes her.
jokes.punchline: Artie's deadpan self-assessment — implying his own comfort with his manipulative mind is a recent achievement — lands as a perfectly dry character button.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — five words that perfectly button a scene and deepen Artie's character. The line implies a history of self-examination about his own ethically dubious methods. Excellent economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Well, there's some chimps at Live at 5 who might be available.

jokes.text: 'Well, there's some chimps at Live at 5 who might be available.' / 'I don't think so.' / 'We'll have to settle for the next-best thing.'
jokes.setup: Paula has exhausted all options. Artie asks if there's truly no one available.
jokes.punchline: Paula offers chimps as a semi-serious alternative. Artie dismisses them — then implies Hank is the 'next-best thing' below chimps. The dismissal of chimps as too good is the actual punchline.
jokes.explanation: A well-structured three-beat joke. The setup is genuine desperation, the chimp offer is the first surprise, and 'we'll have to settle for the next-best thing' is a devastating punchline because the audience already knows the episode is about Hank. The implication — Hank ranks below trained chimps — is delivered without a word of explanation. Sharp, earned comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Paula, are you aware I'm about to open the lid of a box far nastier than Pandora's?

jokes.text: Artie says he's about to 'open the lid of a box far nastier than Pandora's' — then immediately asks for a napkin.
jokes.setup: Artie builds dramatic tension around the terrible decision he's about to make (letting Hank host).
jokes.punchline: The grandiose classical allusion ('a box far nastier than Pandora's') is deflated by the immediate, mundane 'napkin' request — he's mid-bite during this apocalyptic announcement.
jokes.explanation: A lovely piece of comic deflation. The Pandora's box metaphor is both genuinely apt (Hank hosting IS catastrophic) and hilariously portentous — then the napkin breaks the grandiosity perfectly. The joke also works as foreshadowing of the episode's disaster arc.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm not supposed to eat in my show clothes. I know. It's just...I get hungry.

jokes.text: Hank is told he's hosting. His response: 'No.' / 'Yes.' / 'No.' / 'Oh, yes.'
jokes.setup: Artie informs Hank of the opportunity.
jokes.punchline: Hank's binary, childlike oscillation between denial and disbelief before acceptance — four one-word exchanges that speak volumes about his insecurity.
jokes.explanation: Eight words doing the work of a paragraph. The four-beat exchange is perfectly economical — each 'no' reveals something different (shock, disbelief, fear) and the 'Oh, yes' is Hank beginning to believe his luck. Tambor's performance makes this a showcase moment.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: My psychic told me a man in my life was going to be given a great opportunity. I thought she meant my father was going to get a job, but--but this, this is good, too.

jokes.text: 'My psychic told me a man in my life was going to be given a great opportunity. I thought she meant my father was going to get a job, but — but this, this is good, too.'
jokes.setup: Hank processes the news of hosting by recalling a psychic's prediction.
jokes.punchline: The misdirect is the pivot from 'great opportunity' to 'my father getting a job' — the scale deflation (a late-night hosting gig vs. dad finding employment) is both absurd and oddly poignant.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. It's pure character comedy — the psychic detail alone tells us everything about Hank's desperate magical thinking. The pivot to 'my father getting a job' is unexpected and oddly sad, implying a family of underachievers that contextualizes Hank's own insecurity. Then 'this is good, too' nails the self-correcting optimism. This is exactly the kind of joke that only works because of who Hank is. High originality, near-perfect structure, excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I can't move my legs.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Whoop. Hip.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I can't move my legs.' Artie helps him up, calls it 'hip.'
jokes.setup: Hank is so overwhelmed by the news that he physically can't move.
jokes.punchline: Artie's breezy 'Whoop. Hip.' as he physically assists a frozen Hank is the perfect caretaker-of-a-disaster energy.
jokes.explanation: A functional physical beat that's more about Tambor's performance than the writing itself. The comedy is in the image — a paralyzed Hank having to be physically mobilized by his producer — but the writing support is minimal.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm doing some creative visualization, and I'm seeing the audience screaming with laughter.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm seeing the same thing, Darlene.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Thank you for explaining the screaming.

jokes.text: Hank's pre-show to-do list: 'Call my agent, call my manager, call my wife — wife, yes, of course — and I want to eat some fruit. I don't know why... a pineapple.'
jokes.setup: Hank begins rattling off everything he needs to do before the show.
jokes.punchline: The list degrades from professional contacts to 'fruit' — and then the inexplicable specificity of 'a pineapple.' Also, 'wife, yes, of course' reveals she was almost an afterthought.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully observed comic detail. The pineapple is perfectly inexplicable — it doesn't need a reason. 'Wife, yes, of course' is a devastating parenthetical about the state of Hank's marriage. Both gags work independently and together reinforce Hank's chaotic interior.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And, uh, I want to eat some fruit. I don't know why... A pineapple.

jokes.text: Darlene: 'I should call your wife.' Hank: 'Wife, yes. Of course.' Then: 'She has a thing for Hank.' / 'Oh, don't we all?'
jokes.setup: The team processes Hank hosting the show. Darlene notes his wife will be excited.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Oh, don't we all?' is a devastating sarcastic sigh — layered irony given that Artie is the one who just tried to avoid giving Hank this opportunity.
jokes.explanation: Artie's dry sarcasm at his own expense — he's the one who 'has a thing for Hank' in the sense that Hank is his perpetual problem. The line reads differently on rewatch knowing the episode ends with Artie saying he made a mistake.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Artie, my pal, Shadoe Stevens, he's 2 blocks away. Why don't we call him, have him do the warm-up and the intro? Shadoe is 2 blocks away. Did I say that already?

jokes.text: Hank: 'Artie, my pal, Shadoe Stevens, he's 2 blocks away. Why don't we call him, have him do the warm-up and the intro?' Then repeats: 'Shadoe is 2 blocks away. Did I say that already?'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to manage his own anxiety by offloading tasks.
jokes.punchline: The self-aware repetition — 'Did I say that already?' — reveals Hank is so overwhelmed he's lost track of his own words. It's a small panic attack rendered in dialogue.
jokes.explanation: A small but effective character moment — Hank's neurosis manifesting as compulsive repetition. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It's just such a wonderful, tremendous vote of confidence. I want to thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Hank, believe me, I had no choice.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I know. Thank you.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Hank, believe me, I had no choice.' Hank: 'I know. Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Hank thanks Artie for the opportunity.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'I had no choice' is brutal honesty delivered as a compliment, and Hank's gracious acceptance of that backhanded sentiment — 'I know. Thank you' — is either touching or sad depending on how you read it.
jokes.explanation: A gem of cringe comedy. In two exchanges, the show captures the entire Artie/Hank dynamic: Artie's complete honesty (a form of respect) and Hank's willingness to accept any form of validation. 'I know. Thank you' — Hank knows he's the last resort and is grateful anyway. That's genuinely poignant comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Sid
dialogue.line: My, god. Larry's sick?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah. Food poisoning.

dialogue.speaker: Sid
dialogue.line: Didn't anybody tell you?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No!

jokes.text: Hank rehearsing the trunk joke: misunderstands it as Larry literally being in the trunk, rephrases it as 'I put him in the trunk, and I kidnapped him.'
jokes.setup: Phil walks Hank through a monologue joke implying he kidnapped Larry.
jokes.punchline: Hank cannot grasp irony — he keeps literalizing the joke until it becomes a confession rather than a punchline. His 'fix' is funnier than the original.
jokes.explanation: A sustained cringe sequence that's also a masterclass in Hank's character. His inability to understand joke logic — 'there's a logic' — and his 'fix' of spelling out 'I kidnapped him' is both hilarious and deeply revealing. The sequence plays as an extended joke with multiple escalating beats. High character integration: Hank's literal-mindedness is his defining comedic trait.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I guess Artie did, but I was so nervous, and the shock and the excitement, uh...

jokes.text: Phil explaining the trunk joke: 'The idea is that you've kidnapped Larry, and you've put him... in the trunk of my car.' Hank: 'Sheesh. I'm sorry. I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: Phil has to explain to Hank that the joke involves an implied kidnapping.
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'Sheesh. I'm sorry. I'm sorry.' — he's apologizing for not getting the joke, as if his comedic density is a personal failing he should feel bad about.
jokes.explanation: A supporting beat within the trunk joke sequence (joke #20). Hank's cringe-worthy self-flagellation for not understanding comedy is funny but functions as connective tissue rather than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Even though Larry couldn't be here tonight, I know he's comfortable. I have an american car. The trunk is quite spacious.

dialogue.speaker: Sid
dialogue.line: Flip it. No, that's it, Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Sid
dialogue.line: That's the joke.

jokes.text: Artie tells Larry 'everything's going fine' and 'we don't even miss you' on the phone — then immediately says 'we love you, we miss you, you're in our thoughts and prayers.'
jokes.setup: Artie leaves Larry a message while the office is in full panic.
jokes.punchline: The contradiction within the same message — 'we don't even miss you' followed immediately by 'we love you, we miss you' — shows Artie managing Larry's anxiety with deliberate doublespeak.
jokes.explanation: A nice character beat — Artie is simultaneously reassuring and genuine, and the self-contradiction happens within seconds. The joke is in the pace of the reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Even though Larry couldn't be here tonight, I know he's comfortable. I have an american car, and I put him in the trunk, and I kidnapped him.

jokes.text: Phil introduces himself to George Wendt as 'Phil, the best writer.'
jokes.setup: Phil greets the guest star as the bearer of bad news.
jokes.punchline: His self-introduction as 'the best writer' is delivered without irony — a small act of self-aggrandizement that's funny precisely because of how unnecessary and ill-timed it is.
jokes.explanation: A tidy character beat — four words that tell you everything about Phil's psychology. The specificity of the self-designated superlative while delivering crisis news is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Actually, we're off the list--Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: [Retching]

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Larry? Artie, it's Beverly. Larry's vomiting again. Can we get back to you?

jokes.text: George Wendt hears it's Hank hosting: 'Oh, my god. Oh, my god. Well, um... Oh, my god.'
jokes.setup: Phil tells Wendt that Hank is replacing Larry as host.
jokes.punchline: Wendt's triple 'Oh, my god' — each one a different register of existential dread — communicates the full horror without any explicit insult of Hank.
jokes.explanation: The repetition is well-calibrated — three iterations of the same phrase, each slightly differently timed, convey escalating panic. A real actor playing himself allows the joke to be meaner without anyone needing to say anything explicitly mean.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I'm Phil, the best writer. Thanks for doing the show.

dialogue.speaker: George Wendt
dialogue.line: No problem. There's been a little change.

jokes.text: Phil: 'You have a problem with Hank?' Wendt: 'No, no. Hank's great. It's just that it's his first show, and he's a little green.' Phil: 'I did Conan's first show...' Wendt: 'You have to remember.' Phil: 'Yes, I do, and I forgive you.'
jokes.setup: Wendt tries to be diplomatic about Hank's inexperience by comparing him to Conan O'Brien's rocky start.
jokes.punchline: Phil's 'Yes, I do, and I forgive you' — pivoting Wendt's reassurance into a slight against Conan's first show — is a sharp bit of self-deprecating industry humor.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed exchange with a strong punchline. The move from Wendt reassuring Phil about Hank to Phil reassuring Wendt about Conan is elegant. 'I forgive you' implies Conan's first show was also a disaster — a real insider dig that works even without knowing the actual Conan history.

dialogue.speaker: George Wendt
dialogue.line: Who's gonna host? Uh...Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Hank?

dialogue.speaker: George Wendt
dialogue.line: Well, that's cool.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Oh, my god. Oh, my god.

jokes.text: George Wendt mutters 'Shit!' under his breath after leaving the conversation.
jokes.setup: Wendt has put on a professional face for the camera but now believes himself to be unobserved.
jokes.punchline: The unguarded moment — a single expletive that summarizes everything he couldn't say diplomatically — is the real review of Hank's appointment.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word as punctuation to the entire scene. It's the verbal equivalent of a slow deflation. Works best in context immediately after the diplomatic scene.

dialogue.speaker: George Wendt
dialogue.line: I did Conan's first show, so... You have to remember.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Yes, I do, and I forgive you.

jokes.text: The written intro: 'Because everybody else in show business was out of town or in rehab — Hey, now! Hey — hey, now! Hank Kingsley!'
jokes.setup: Phil reads the written introduction for Hank.
jokes.punchline: The announced reason for Hank's presence — 'everybody else was out of town or in rehab' — is the premise itself delivered as a joke, making the show's desperation the punchline.
jokes.explanation: The self-awareness of the intro is sharp — making the show's casting failure into the opening joke. It's also a meta joke about late-night show desperation. 'In rehab' is the period-specific kicker.

dialogue.speaker: Shadoe Stevens
dialogue.line: Kings...Kingsley! Kings-leyyyy! Kind of a flaired-out riff. No. B-flat. Kings-ley! Kings-leyyyyy!

jokes.text: Shadoe Stevens coaching Hank on the two-note inflection of 'Kings-LEYYY!' with musical precision — 'Kind of a flaired-out riff. No. B-flat.'
jokes.setup: Shadoe is helping Hank perfect his intro announcement.
jokes.punchline: The absurd musicological precision applied to shouting a man's name — 'B-flat' — is funny as a collision of professional seriousness and trivial subject matter.
jokes.explanation: A nice absurdist beat. The comedy is in the disproportionate expertise brought to bear on an essentially meaningless task. Shadoe Stevens playing himself with total earnestness amplifies the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm just trying to pick out the right tie for the show. What about this one? You think that one?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, definitely.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Ok. That's the one. You're the boss.

jokes.text: Artie says 'Love you on Dave's World, kiddo' to Shadoe Stevens.
jokes.setup: Artie wraps up a brief interaction with Shadoe.
jokes.punchline: Artie calls Shadoe 'kiddo' and compliments him on a B-level CBS sitcom in the same breath — warmly dismissive, it's an industry veteran acknowledging a journeyman's work with gentle condescension.
jokes.explanation: A mild but characterful aside. The joke is partly in knowing Dave's World was a forgettable sitcom — the compliment is faint praise from someone who's seen real talent. Works better with era-specific knowledge.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And, uh, you know, I ordered some pineapple. Have you seen my pineapple?

jokes.text: Hank's pre-show breakdown: 'Don't make me do this. I'm not up to this. Don't make me.' / 'What if I suck?' repeated three times.
jokes.setup: Minutes before air, Hank spirals into existential panic.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'What if I suck?' as the core fear — stripped of any euphemism — is simultaneously funny and genuinely affecting. The loop of the phrase amplifies both.
jokes.explanation: This extended cringe sequence works because 'What if I suck?' is simultaneously the episode's funniest line and its most honest one. Hank's self-awareness about potential failure — and his wish to avoid ever finding out — is tragicomic in the best Larry Sanders tradition. High character integration, genuinely earned.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Don't make me do this. Ok? I just can't do this. I'm not... I'm not up to this. Don't make me.

jokes.text: Artie's pre-show pep talk: 'I been in this business, man and boy, almost 40 years. I know things, Hank. Let me tell you one of the things I know. You do not suck!'
jokes.setup: Artie tries to give Hank a stirring pep talk seconds before air.
jokes.punchline: The grandiose build-up ('man and boy, almost 40 years... I know things') pays off with the most unpoetic possible confidence booster: 'You do not suck.' The negative framing is the joke — he can't even say 'You're great.'
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. The structure is immaculate: a 40-year credential drop, a portentous 'I know things,' and then the payoff lands in the lowest possible register — 'You do not suck.' It's perfect because it's both genuinely encouraging (Artie means it) and damning (he literally cannot muster better). Hank's response — 'That's one of the kindest things anyone has ever said to me' — is the callback that seals it. This is the caliber of an 8.0 anchor or better: memorable, character-specific, perfectly structured, deeply quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What if I suck?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Never!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah, what if I suck? After all this time, I finally get my chance, and what if I just suck?

jokes.text: Hank: 'That's one of the kindest things anyone has ever said to me.' [Applause begins]
jokes.setup: Artie delivers his 'you do not suck' pep talk.
jokes.punchline: Hank receives 'you do not suck' as among the kindest things ever said to him — revealing the poverty of encouragement he's received throughout his career.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to joke #33. Structurally, this is the button that makes the pep talk into a complete two-beat joke. Hank's sincere reception of 'you do not suck' as profound kindness is both hilarious and heartbreaking — it implies a lifetime of receiving worse. These two jokes together form the episode's comedic peak.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What are you drinking?

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Red zinger and gin.

jokes.text: Hank delivers the trunk joke on air: 'I have an American car, and the trunk is quite spacious.' [Laughter]
jokes.setup: After the extended rehearsal scene where Hank couldn't understand the joke, he now delivers it live.
jokes.punchline: The callback to the rehearsal — he got it right — is the meta-joke. The joke itself is mild, but the context of watching Hank successfully execute something he couldn't understand is the real payoff.
jokes.explanation: The payoff works through dramatic context rather than intrinsic joke quality. The audience's relief that Hank pulls it off — after watching him fail so badly in rehearsal — earns the laugh. The joke itself is only okay, but the callback structure elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I been in this business, man and boy, almost 40 years. I know things, Hank. Let me tell you one of the things I know. You do not suck!

jokes.text: Hank's monologue joke: 'Tennis star Jennifer Capriati is in drug rehab. I mean, is this really a surprise? I seem to remember people all the time saying she preferred playing on grass.'
jokes.setup: Hank delivers a topical monologue joke about a real celebrity.
jokes.punchline: 'Playing on grass' — the tennis surface double-meaning as marijuana pun.
jokes.explanation: This is an intentionally weak joke — it's a mid-'90s late-night monologue pun that the show presents as getting a real audience laugh. The wordplay is obvious and the structure is rote. Low craft scores are appropriate because the show is partially commenting on how generic monologue comedy is. Still functional enough to land.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Now, before we goes... Before we goes on...

jokes.text: Artie watching Hank get his first big laugh: 'Good for Hank.' / 'You don't understand. This is going to go right to his head. He's going to be a huge, huge pain in the ass. You know Jimmy Woods? That's nothing.'
jokes.setup: Hank gets his first laugh from the audience. Someone says 'Good for Hank.'
jokes.punchline: Artie's immediate reframe — the laugh is catastrophic because it will empower Hank, and comparing the incoming ego to James Woods ('that's nothing') is both a dig at Woods and a terrifying prophecy.
jokes.explanation: A superb joke because it works on two levels: it's funny as an industry dig at James Woods (a notorious difficult actor) and it's also perfect Artie characterization — his first response to success is dread. The James Woods comparison is so specific it feels real, and it immediately raises stakes for the back half of the episode. This is the joke that tells the audience what's coming.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Even though Larry wouldn't be... couldn't be here tonight, I know he's comfortable. I have an american car, and the trunk is quite spacious.

jokes.text: Hank on air: 'My father always told me to tell the truth. So if it isn't obvious, I'm really terrified. So you're probably not going to see a really great show tonight.'
jokes.setup: Hank pivots from his monologue to direct address with the audience.
jokes.punchline: Admitting terror and preemptively lowering expectations for the show while doing the show — self-deprecation as performance strategy, and it works.
jokes.explanation: This is a beautiful moment because it's both the funniest and truest thing Hank can say. The honesty disarms the audience and demonstrates the episode's key thesis — vulnerability is Hank's superpower. The joke writes itself from the character's deepest truth. High earned vs. cheap score.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Tennis star Jennifer Capriati is in the drug rehab. I mean, is this really a surprise? I seem to remember people all the time saying she preferred playing on grass.

jokes.text: Audience begins chanting 'Hank! Hank! Hank!' — Hank is visibly overwhelmed.
jokes.setup: Hank's honesty wins the audience over completely.
jokes.punchline: The absurd reversal — a man who was paralyzed with fear 90 seconds ago now has the crowd chanting his name — is the comedic/dramatic payoff to the entire first act.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is structural and cumulative — the payoff to the entire pre-show anxiety sequence. The chanting is earned dramatically, making it funny rather than purely triumphant. The image of an overwhelmed Hank being chanted at is pure character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: He just got his first big laugh. Good for Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You don't understand. This is gonna go right to his head.

jokes.text: Hank's on-air interview begins and he immediately reads questions directly from index cards. George Wendt breaks: 'Hank, what are you doing with those cards?'
jokes.setup: Hank sits down for the interview segment, apparently recovered.
jokes.punchline: He immediately ruins the vibe by robotically reading from cards — so transparently bad at interviewing that even his guest breaks character to call it out.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed cringe moment. The irony is that Hank just won the crowd with vulnerability, then immediately retreats into mechanical safety. The reversal is fast and sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You know, my father always told me to tell the truth, so if it isn't obvious, I'm really terrified. So you're probably not going to see a really great show tonight.

jokes.text: Wendt grabs Hank's cards: 'They're a crutch! Larry needs the cards. This man doesn't need them.' Hank: 'I need the cards.'
jokes.setup: Wendt tries to free Hank from the cards by insulting Larry.
jokes.punchline: Hank insists he needs the cards while Wendt claims he doesn't — the irony being that Hank absolutely does need them, and the audience knows it. Also, 'Larry needs the cards' is a casually brutal aside about the host.
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe/character beat. The dig at Larry ('Larry needs the cards') is a sleeper joke embedded in the chaos — it punctures Larry's image without Larry being present.

dialogue.speaker: Audience
dialogue.line: Go, Hank, go! [Chanting] Hank! Hank! Hank!

jokes.text: Artie's post-show assessment: 'I have to be honest. I thought we were going to have to warn people to watch the show through a pin hole and a piece of cardboard.'
jokes.setup: Hank wraps the show successfully. Artie congratulates him.
jokes.punchline: Artie's solar-eclipse metaphor — the show was so expected to be terrible that viewers would need protective eyewear — is both inventive and perfectly Artie.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent metaphor joke. The solar-eclipse comparison is unexpected, visually vivid, and perfectly calibrated — Artie thought Hank would be so bad that watching would cause permanent damage. The elevated image (pin hole and cardboard) applied to TV watching is inventive and original. High across the board.

dialogue.speaker: George Wendt
dialogue.line: Hank, cards are a crutch. They're a crutch. There goes-- Thank you and good night. Hank, you don't need the cards.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Now I know why Larry is so puffed up.'
jokes.setup: Hank basks in post-show adulation.
jokes.punchline: The unguarded observation — one successful night has already given Hank enough ego to diagnose Larry's — is a quick, pointed character beat that sets up the episode's second act.
jokes.explanation: A compact and effective transitional joke. The dramatic irony is rich — Hank has NO idea how quickly this self-insight will become self-indictment.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I have to be honest. I thought we were going to have to warn people to watch this show through a pin hole and a piece of cardboard.

jokes.text: Beverly's morning update: Larry 'ran into the bathroom, slipped and fell, and hit his head on the john. It's a minor concussion, but it's serious enough to get those pain killers he's been after.'
jokes.setup: The morning after, Beverly updates Artie on Larry's condition.
jokes.punchline: The cascade of misfortune culminates in the darkly funny detail that the concussion was 'serious enough to get those pain killers he's been after' — implying Larry has been seeking opioids and only a head injury could justify the prescription.
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy at its best — the reveal that Larry's head injury is a silver lining (pain pills) is both awful and funny. The matter-of-fact delivery from Beverly amplifies the darkly satirical take on celebrity hypochondria and substance use.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I have to be honest. I thought we were going to have to warn people to watch this show through a pin hole and a piece of cardboard.

jokes.text: Hank swans in with 'Yay! He's here, everybody! Yay!' being called out around the office — a hero's welcome he's clearly enjoying too much.
jokes.setup: Hank arrives at the office the morning after his successful show.
jokes.punchline: The exaggerated welcome — which the audience suspects is partly genuine and partly Hank's projection — and Hank's visible relishing of it sets up every joke that follows.
jokes.explanation: More of a scene-setter than a standalone joke, but Hank's triumphalist entrance is comedically effective as contrast to his terrified pre-show state. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Now I know why Larry is so puffed up.

jokes.text: Random staffer to Hank: 'You were great last night, Hank. As good as Larry, maybe even better.'
jokes.setup: Staff congratulate Hank.
jokes.punchline: The gratuitous 'maybe even better' — going further than necessary — is the kind of sycophancy that will fuel Hank's delusion. It's a joke about the ecosystem of flattery around TV hosts.
jokes.explanation: A functional background gag about television flattery culture. Not particularly crafted, but serves the episode's satirical purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Well, Artie, he's over that food poisoning, but last night, he ran into the bathroom, and he slipped and fell and hit his head on the john.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Still flushed with victory?' Hank: 'Yes, I am flushed with victory. You sound a little surprised I did so well.' Artie: 'Oh? I'm glad I'm not playing poker anytime soon.'
jokes.setup: Artie checks in with Hank the morning after.
jokes.punchline: Artie's poker-face reference — he cannot conceal his surprise — is dry, self-aware, and perfectly delivered. He's admitting he was wrong without actually admitting he was wrong.
jokes.explanation: Artie's capacity for oblique honesty is one of the show's signature pleasures. 'I'm glad I'm not playing poker' — as a way of saying 'I clearly misjudged you' — is both charming and funny. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: It's serious enough to get those pain killers he's been after. Yay!

jokes.text: Talent booker tells Hank 'You were great' — Hank immediately asks her to get him a coffee. 'No. No, I book talent. I don't get coffee.'
jokes.setup: Hank accepts congratulations from the talent booker.
jokes.punchline: Hank has been a TV host for one night and is already expecting coffee service from senior staff — revealing how instantly intoxicating the power is.
jokes.explanation: A sharp character beat. Hank's entitlement flares up instantly — the 'you were great/get me a coffee' pivot is barely a beat apart. The booker's flat refusal and job description ('I book talent') is a perfect deadpan put-down.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You sound a little surprised I did so well.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh? I'm glad I'm not playing poker anytime soon.

jokes.text: 'Then could you book David Copperfield on the show, and when he gets here, have him pull a cup of coffee out of his ass?'
jokes.setup: The booker refuses to get coffee. Hank tries to find a workaround.
jokes.punchline: Hank's solution: book a world-famous magician specifically to conjure coffee from his own rectum. The specificity of the logistics — and the deadpan earnestness — makes this absurdist and funny.
jokes.explanation: An excellent absurdist joke. The comedic concept is original (using professional booking channels to procure a magical coffee solution), the image is vivid, and Hank's escalating pique makes the absurdity feel earned rather than random. 'Decaf?' as the booker's reply pushes it further — she'll negotiate the terms of an impossible request rather than simply laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: No. No, I book talent. I don't get coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Then could you book David Copperfield on the show, and when he gets here, have him pull a cup of coffee out of his ass?

jokes.text: Booker: 'Decaf?' (in response to the David Copperfield/ass coffee request)
jokes.setup: Hank demands magically-produced coffee.
jokes.punchline: The booker's only question is the type of coffee — she's treating an impossible request with complete professional seriousness.
jokes.explanation: One word doing maximum comedy work. The entire joke is in the implication — she's not questioning the method of delivery, only the specifications. The economy is near-perfect (9.5). This is the button that makes joke #49 into a genuinely great two-beat sequence. The best short punchline of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, correct me if I'm wrong, but the procedure is the guest host gets to use Larry's office, right?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Yes. The guest host, which you are not.

jokes.text: Hank's phone call with Larry — Larry congratulates him, Hank says 'You left me some mighty big shoes to fill.' Larry: 'Come on, come on.' Hank: 'That's very nice of you.' / 'No one can do this show quite like you.'
jokes.setup: Larry calls Hank post-show to congratulate him.
jokes.punchline: The sycophancy flows both ways — Hank says 'mighty big shoes,' Larry demurs, Hank says 'that's very nice of you' (accepting the deflection as modesty), and Larry reasserts his own irreplaceability. Both men are performing for each other.
jokes.explanation: A good character beat about the mutual performance between host and sidekick. Larry's 'no one can do this show quite like you' — ostensibly a compliment — is really a reassertion of his own primacy. Both men understand the subtext.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Because if I do, you know he'll give me the go-ahead to kick your balls right out through the top of your head!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, language!

jokes.text: Hank is discovered sitting in Larry's chair at Larry's desk. 'Well, correct me if I'm wrong, but the procedure is the guest host gets to use Larry's office, right?'
jokes.setup: Artie finds Hank installed in Larry's office as if he belongs there.
jokes.punchline: Hank's confident appeal to 'the procedure' — an invented norm he states as fact — reveals he has already mentally redecorated Larry's life as his own.
jokes.explanation: A strong character comedy beat. The absurd self-assurance of 'the procedure' — there is no procedure, he made it up — shows Hank rationalizing his power grab as institutional. It's the episode's first real evidence of the ego corruption Artie predicted.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey. Hey, I saved your asses last night. This is the--the fucking gratitude I get?

jokes.text: Hank: 'I'd appreciate it if you switched desks with Darlene. I'd like her a little closer to me today.'
jokes.setup: Having claimed Larry's office, Hank begins reorganizing the staff.
jokes.punchline: The casual authority of requesting a desk swap — mid-sentence, as if it's already decided — shows Hank sliding deeper into host-character. The escalation from office to desk reorganization is fast and funny.
jokes.explanation: Part of the escalating Hank-goes-power-mad sequence. Works as escalation comedy — each new demand is slightly more absurd than the last.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: 'Kingsley proved himself completely maladroit in the host's chair.' Hank, 'adroit' means 'able.' 'Mal' means 'bad' or 'not.' Put 'em together. Maladroit--not able. capisce?

jokes.text: Beverly threatens to call Larry: 'You know he'll give me the go-ahead to kick your balls right out through the top of your head!' Hank: 'Oh, language!'
jokes.setup: Beverly loses patience with Hank's office takeover.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's anatomically creative threat — which is disproportionately violent for an office dispute — is funny for its hyperbole. Hank's prim 'Oh, language!' in response to a man who has been casually crude all episode is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: The reversal is the joke: Beverly goes violent, Hank goes genteel. 'Oh, language!' from a man who said 'fucking' ten minutes ago is perfectly hypocritical. The threat itself is vivid enough to be funny on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, it's funny because last week, Larry and Arthur were talking, and one of them said that they thought the whole neurotic Jewish person thing that you do is, uh-- What'd he say? Predictably, uh, banal.

jokes.text: Hank: 'This is the fucking gratitude I get? I mean, come on. Look in front of your face. It's me, ok? It's Hank Kingsley. I can do this job.'
jokes.setup: Hank discovers Richard Lewis is hosting tonight and loses his composure.
jokes.punchline: 'Look in front of your face. It's me, ok? It's Hank Kingsley.' — delivered as if his own name is the clinching argument. The phrase 'look in front of your face' is almost grammatically wrong, which amplifies the desperation.
jokes.explanation: Tambor territory — the self-announcement ('It's Hank Kingsley') as argument is pure character comedy. The speech is both completely understandable (he did save the show) and completely unhinged (he's behaving like a diva). High character integration because no other character on this show would announce themselves by name as their strongest credential.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: The whole neurotic Jewish person thing that you do is, uh-- What'd he say? Predictably, uh, banal.

jokes.text: Hank reads a positive review: 'Kingsley's winning demeanor took Sanders' place with relative ease' — then reads a negative one: 'Kingsley proved himself completely maladroit in the host's chair'
jokes.setup: Hank is making his case using newspaper reviews
jokes.punchline: He quotes a negative review without realizing it's negative — 'maladroit' reads to him as a positive because it sounds like 'adroit'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best constructed jokes. The structure is perfect: positive review read with satisfaction, negative review read with equal satisfaction, followed by Artie's word-by-word etymology lesson. The punchline is that Hank is simultaneously proving the reviewer right (he lacks sophistication) while thinking he's disproving them. 'Mal means bad or not. Put 'em together. Maladroit — not able. Capisce?' delivered by Artie as patient instruction is devastating.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm sure Hank got on the phone with him. That crazy son of a bitch. I don't think Richard's that crazy. I think that's just an act. I meant Hank.

jokes.text: Hank reading reviews: 'Kingsley's winning demeanor took Sanders' place with relative ease.' Then: 'Kingsley proved himself completely maladroit in the host's chair.'
jokes.setup: Hank selectively reads reviews to make his case for hosting again.
jokes.punchline: The second review appears to be positive but 'maladroit' means inept — Hank has been quoting a devastating review as evidence of his brilliance.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed vocabulary joke. The structure is perfect: Hank reads the word 'maladroit' without knowing what it means, uses it as evidence in an argument, and has to be corrected by Artie. It's both a vocabulary joke and a character joke — Hank's overconfidence in his own comprehension is the engine. The follow-up ('capisce?') makes Artie's correction a small act of performative condescension.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Last night he was a crying mess... Now he's the ass of the western world.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Hank, 'adroit' means 'able.' 'Mal' means 'bad' or 'not.' Put 'em together. Maladroit — not able. Capisce?'
jokes.setup: Hank has cited a negative review as proof of his talent.
jokes.punchline: Artie's patient, almost pedagogical breakdown of the word — as if to a child — followed by the Italian 'capisce?' is condescending and funny. The word dissection is funnier because Artie does it with complete composure.
jokes.explanation: Artie's etymology lesson is both funny for its content and its tone. 'Capisce?' is perfect: it implies that Italian is clearer than English for someone this dense. The two-joke sequence (#56 and #57) is among the episode's better constructed bits.

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: I think socks had something to do with that decision.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It's not funny. I beg your pardon? What word do you have trouble with? You understand 'not'? That's comfortable for you? And 'funny.' You've heard of that?

jokes.text: Reaction beat: Hank goes silent after being corrected about 'maladroit.' Long pause before Beverly says 'Get Larry on the phone.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just explained that the review Hank cited as praise was actually devastating.
jokes.punchline: The silence that follows — Hank processing that he publicly argued using his own negative review as evidence — is the punchline. The world pauses to let the humiliation sink in.
jokes.explanation: The silence here does more work than dialogue could. It's the moment of complete deflation — Hank's entire argument has collapsed, and the beat lets the audience savor the absurdity. Beverly's businesslike 'Get Larry on the phone' stepping into the void is the perfect functional button. High economy score for the comedic value of nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: What? What?! You've changed, Hank. There's a darkness around you.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Good, fine. There's a darkness.

jokes.text: Richard Lewis to Hank: 'Question — are you gonna be doing your usual shtick?' ... 'It's funny, because last week, Larry and Arthur were talking, and one of them said that they thought the whole neurotic Jewish person thing that you do is... predictably banal.'
jokes.setup: Hank has called Richard Lewis, ostensibly to congratulate him on hosting. Actually, Hank is trying to destabilize Lewis.
jokes.punchline: Hank weaponizes an invented quote about Richard Lewis's entire comedic persona being 'predictably banal' — attributed to the people Lewis works for. It's a fully formed act of sabotage delivered with friendly concern.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant piece of character-driven dark comedy. Hank's psychological sabotage of Lewis — performed as a concerned phone call — is both funny and genuinely disturbing. The specificity of 'the neurotic Jewish person thing' is a real meta-joke about Lewis's actual persona, and 'predictably banal' is the right level of intellectual-sounding devastation for an insecure comedian to internalize. High character integration: this move is distinctly Hank — not malicious genius, just desperate enough to try.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I prayed. I mean, I actually got down on my knees, and I prayed that Larry would stay sick so I could host the show tonight. I mean, I wished this man unwell.

jokes.text: Hank calls Richard Lewis before Lewis hosts, asking if he'll 'be doing your usual shtick' — then relays that Larry and Artie called Richard's 'whole neurotic Jewish person thing' 'predictably banal'
jokes.setup: Hank undermines Richard Lewis's confidence before his hosting appearance
jokes.punchline: Hank weaponizes invented criticism — attributing to Larry and Artie the opinion that Richard's entire persona is 'predictably banal' — which is sabotage disguised as concern, delivered with the plausible deniability of 'one of them said'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's darkest and best jokes. Hank's sabotage is so transparently self-interested, so clumsily executed ('I don't want to get into this... it's funny because last week...'), and so hilariously specific ('the whole neurotic Jewish person thing') that it crosses from cringe into genuine comedy villain territory. The phrase 'predictably banal' in Hank's mouth is funny because it's clearly not his vocabulary — he's quoting (or inventing) a criticism he barely understands. Exceptional character work.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: See, that's interesting because I told our head writer that that was, you know, a little off, but he's such a hopeless retard that...

jokes.text: Artie: 'I pass out unexpectedly, but other than that, I feel better than the night we had Jennifer Tilly on.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks how Artie is doing.
jokes.punchline: Two jokes stacked: (1) 'I pass out unexpectedly' as a casual health disclosure that Artie considers minor, and (2) the comparison to Jennifer Tilly's appearance as a medical nadir — whatever happened that night, it was worse than random blackouts.
jokes.explanation: A superb Artie line. The casualness of 'I pass out unexpectedly' is Rip Torn comedy gold — it's a major health symptom treated as a minor inconvenience, which tells you everything about Artie. The Jennifer Tilly comparison elevates it further: an unexplained specific reference that implies a legendary bad episode. The audience doesn't need to know what happened — the specificity is funny enough.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You see, it's not Larry who is sick. It's me. Yes, it's me. I am very sick. I am a sicko. I'm so fucking sick. But I'm finally where I belong.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I don't say this often, Larry, but I made a mistake. I should have canceled last night's show instead of putting Hank on. Last night he was a crying mess... [thud] Oh! Now he's the ass of the western world.'
jokes.setup: Artie admits his error in letting Hank host.
jokes.punchline: 'The ass of the western world' — Artie's heightened, old-world phrasing for 'insufferable egomaniac' — is funny in its grandeur. The [thud] mid-sentence (presumably Artie dropping something or falling) is either a physical gag or a stress response, both of which are funny.
jokes.explanation: 'The ass of the western world' is one of the episode's more quotable Artie-isms. The contrast between 'crying mess' (last night) and 'ass of the western world' (this morning) captures the show's key irony beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm sure socks had something to do with that decision. See, that's interesting because I told our head writer that that was, you know, a little off, but he's such a hopeless retard that...

jokes.text: The monologue joke argument between Artie and the writer Sid: 'I think socks had something to do with that decision.' / 'It's not funny. I beg your pardon? What word do you have trouble with? You understand 'not'? That's comfortable for you? And 'funny.' You've heard of that?'
jokes.setup: Artie and Sid are arguing about whether a Clinton/socks joke is funny.
jokes.punchline: Artie's rhetorical deconstruction of 'not funny' — treating it as if Sid couldn't parse either word — is simultaneously condescending and hilarious. The mock-Socratic 'you've heard of that?' is the button.
jokes.explanation: Artie's professorial condescension toward the writing staff is a recurring pleasure, and this is a particularly well-constructed example. The pedagogical breakdown of 'not funny' into its component syllables is genuinely funny writing.

dialogue.speaker: Audience member
dialogue.line: You suck!

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Take a seat.

jokes.text: Artie: 'You may go.' Writer: 'Oh, may I? Thank you.' Then, after leaving, under breath: 'Watch it, asshole.'
jokes.setup: Artie dismisses Sid with royal prerogative.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate show of deference ('Oh, may I? Thank you') masks the writer's genuine contempt — the muttered 'asshole' is the real response, delivered once safely out of range.
jokes.explanation: A small but effective structural joke about workplace power dynamics. The formal courtesy covering real contempt is a sitcom staple, but this version is executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, no, Hank. It really got away. It's down in Bolivia by now.

jokes.text: Hank confronting Darlene: 'You've changed, Hank. There's a darkness around you.' Hank: 'Good, fine. There's a darkness.'
jokes.setup: Darlene voices concern about Hank's behavior.
jokes.punchline: Hank's flat acceptance and even endorsement of 'there's a darkness around you' — rather than denial — shows how far gone he is. He takes it as a compliment.
jokes.explanation: A tight, well-constructed character moment. Hank receiving 'there's a darkness around you' with satisfaction rather than alarm is both funny and unsettling — his arc in this episode is essentially a one-day slide into vanity and megalomania.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You should send 3 baskets to Lionel Richie, one for each time you called him Little Richard.

jokes.text: Hank's confession to Darlene: 'I prayed. I actually got down on my knees, and I prayed that Larry would stay sick so I could host the show tonight. I mean, I wished this man unwell.'
jokes.setup: Hank has a moment of self-awareness with Darlene.
jokes.punchline: The admission is darkly funny because it's so earnest — 'I wished this man unwell' as a formal articulation of ordinary workplace envy — and the kneeling prayer detail makes it absurdly theatrical.
jokes.explanation: The formal language of sin applied to petty workplace ambition is the joke. 'I wished this man unwell' is a precise, slightly archaic phrasing that makes the mundane psychology sound operatic. High character integration — this is the dark side of the 'what if I suck' speech earlier.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: When you're vulnerable and humble, people like you. When you act like an asshole, people tend to think of you as an asshole.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I'm still doing it. I hope he gets sick through the weekend and on until the week after that and the week after that.' Darlene: 'Hank, don't!' Hank: 'You don't get it, do you? You see, it's not Larry who is sick. It's me. Yes, it's me. I am very sick. I am a sicko. I'm so fucking sick. But I'm finally where I belong.'
jokes.setup: Hank reveals he's still actively praying for Larry's illness.
jokes.punchline: The escalating self-diagnosis — 'very sick,' 'sicko,' 'so fucking sick' — climaxes with 'but I'm finally where I belong,' which reframes the pathology as fulfillment. It's simultaneously cringe comedy, dark comedy, and a genuine character revelation.
jokes.explanation: The episode's thematic and comedic climax. The speech earns its length because each beat reveals something new: first he admits ongoing prayer, then self-diagnosis, then the twist — 'I'm finally where I belong.' The escalation from 'very sick' to 'sicko' to 'so fucking sick' is perfectly calibrated, and the final line recontextualizes everything as not pathology but destiny. This is the kind of sustained character comedy that defines The Larry Sanders Show at its best. Near-perfect structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: when you're sick that close to air, we'll cancel. Hank's place is on the couch where he does his best work. And always let Beverly go into that yogurt shop alone.

jokes.text: Hank's second show monologue: 'President Clinton announced we'll be trading tuna with the Japanese. I'm sure Socks had something to do with that decision.' [Light laughter, then woman laughs loudly]
jokes.setup: Hank opens his second night monologue with a topical joke.
jokes.punchline: The joke is intentionally mediocre — the punchline attributing trade policy to the President's cat is barely a joke. The sparse audience reaction (one woman laughing) is the real punchline.
jokes.explanation: This joke is intentionally bad — the show is depicting Hank bombing. The low craft scores are appropriate and even necessary: the comedy of the scene depends on the audience knowing the monologue is bad. The callback to the Artie/Sid argument about whether this joke works pays off with the answer: it doesn't. Scored low by design.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'll admit, I may have mishandled this affair, but everything turned out for the best.

jokes.text: Hank calls his writer 'a hopeless retard' on live television — audience groans — man yells 'You suck!'
jokes.setup: Hank is explaining why a bad joke was in the monologue
jokes.punchline: The slur causes an immediate audience groan and a 'you suck!' from the crowd — the joke is the speed and scale of the self-destruction, happening live on air in real time
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the speed and completeness of Hank's implosion — from mediocre joke to slur to audience revolt in about thirty seconds. The joke is not the slur itself but the trajectory: Hank trying to recover from a bad joke and making it catastrophically worse. The 'you suck' callback to Hank's earlier 'what if I suck?' gives it a tragic ironic dimension.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hey, Artie? What's happenin'?

jokes.text: Heck from the audience: 'You suck!'
jokes.setup: Hank has just used a slur on air and the audience is groaning.
jokes.punchline: The echo of the episode's central anxiety — 'what if I suck?' — delivered by a stranger in the audience as prediction fulfilled. It's a callback to joke #31 by the universe itself.
jokes.explanation: Two words that close the episode's primary comedic loop. Hank's paralyzing pre-show fear — 'what if I suck?' — is answered here with brutal, public simplicity. The structural elegance of the callback is what earns the high score: everything Hank feared came true, delivered in exactly the words he used to describe it. Perfect economy, perfect structure. The funniest and saddest moment of the episode simultaneously.

jokes.text: Artie's disciplinary list: 'You will issue an apology about the remarks about the mentally challenged. A healthy donation to, let's say, the Down Syndrome people wouldn't hurt. But you should send a gift basket to John Cusack about that remark you made about his sister. And you should send 3 baskets to Lionel Richie, one for each time you called him Little Richard.'
jokes.setup: Artie delineates the damage Hank caused during his second show.
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of celebrity offenses — each more absurd than the last — with the specific quantification (three baskets for three offenses against Lionel Richie) is both satirically sharp and structurally funny.
jokes.explanation: The list joke is a comedy workhorse, but this is a particularly well-loaded version. The gift-basket-to-John-Cusack detail is unexpectedly specific (why his sister? we'll never know, and that's funnier). 'One for each time you called him Little Richard' — the accounting of the offenses against Lionel Richie — shows Artie's meticulous crisis management, which is both a character joke and a satire of celebrity PR. High quotability.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Now, Hank, what have we learned here? When you're vulnerable and humble, people like you. When you act like an asshole, people tend to think of you as an asshole.'
jokes.setup: Artie delivers the episode's moral to a chastened Hank.
jokes.punchline: The lesson is so basic as to be absurdist — Artie is literally explaining kindergarten social ethics as if it were industry wisdom.
jokes.explanation: The symmetry of 'when you act like an asshole, people tend to think of you as an asshole' has the rhythm and force of an aphorism. It's delivered by a man who is often himself an asshole, which adds irony. A well-constructed Artie speech button.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Are you going to air tonight's show?' 'No. We'll put on the best of Larry. But I'll always have a copy of tonight's show close by. Just keep that in mind next time you want to throw your weight around.'
jokes.setup: Hank asks if the show will air.
jokes.punchline: Artie's power move — keeping a tape of Hank's disaster as blackmail material — delivered casually as a management strategy. The casualness makes it more menacing and more funny.
jokes.explanation: The threat of archiving humiliation as a management tool is both funny and entirely plausible in Hollywood. The line reveals Artie's ultimate power — he controls not just the show but the narrative of Hank's history. High character integration: this is exactly what Artie would do.

jokes.text: Larry on speakerphone after Hank exits: 'Is he gone yet?' / 'Don't let the doorknob hit you in the ass.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just been dismissed from Artie's office.
jokes.punchline: Larry's voice emerging from the speakerphone reveals he was listening the entire time — and his 'don't let the doorknob hit you in the ass' is both a cliché deployed with perfect timing and evidence that Larry has been silently enjoying Hank's dressing-down.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Larry was on the speakerphone the whole time is a great structural surprise. The character insight is sharp: Larry is sick in bed, but he couldn't resist listening to Hank get destroyed. 'Is he gone yet?' is the paranoid, controlling Larry we know. The cliché 'don't let the doorknob hit you' gets a revival from perfect timing and the Larry reveal.

jokes.text: Artie's closing three lessons: '1 — when you're sick that close to air, we'll cancel. 2 — Hank's place is on the couch where he does his best work. And 3 — always let Beverly go into that yogurt shop alone.'
jokes.setup: Artie delivers his post-episode debrief to Larry.
jokes.punchline: Lesson 3 — returning to the yogurt shop that started the whole episode — is the callback that closes the structural loop. The absurdity of converting a food poisoning incident into formal institutional policy is funny. Also, lesson 2 — 'Hank's place is on the couch' — is a crisp industry put-down.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured callback sequence. The three-lesson format (management-speak applied to chaos) is inherently funny, and lesson 3 returning to the yogurt shop closes the episode's structural circle. The joke requires having seen the whole episode, which is high-level sitcom craft. 'Hank's place is on the couch where he does his best work' is a devastating one-sentence career assessment.

jokes.text: Artie's three lessons: 1) Cancel when sick close to air, 2) Hank belongs on the couch, 3) 'Always let Beverly go into that yogurt shop alone'
jokes.setup: Artie summarizes the episode's learnings for Larry
jokes.punchline: The third lesson — sending Beverly in alone to the yogurt shop — is a callback to the episode's inciting incident, delivered as a procedural safety tip for future shows. The comedy is in reducing the whole episode to a personnel policy about frozen yogurt.
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing callback is perfectly structured: two genuine lessons followed by the absurd third lesson (yogurt shop policy) that reduces the entire chaos of Hank's one-night ego trip to a footnote about Larry's frozen yogurt habits. It's the right note to end on — returning to the mundane while acknowledging the insanity.

jokes.text: Artie's closing self-assessment: 'I'll admit, I may have mishandled this affair, but everything turned out for the best. And I think you see that it's gonna be all right.' [Thud] 'Oh!' Larry: 'You agree, right? Hey, Artie? What's happenin'?'
jokes.setup: Artie wraps up the episode with confident self-assessment.
jokes.punchline: The [thud] + 'Oh!' — Artie appears to have fallen or dropped something, possibly passed out (echoing his earlier comment about unexpected blackouts). Then Larry calling into the void echoes the episode's opening scene. The callback to 'I pass out unexpectedly' is unspoken but structurally perfect.
jokes.explanation: The episode ends on a perfect dark-comedy button: Artie's triumphant self-assessment is undercut by what appears to be a blackout or fall. The callback to 'I pass out unexpectedly' (said earlier as an aside) suddenly becomes ominous. 'Hey, Artie? What's happenin'?' mirrors the chaos-management tone of the whole episode — now Artie is the one who needs managing. Structurally elegant as a closing joke.

tmdb_overview: Hank gets his shot at the big chair when Larry gets food poisoning just before a taping.
